title: NIST SP 800-61 Incident Handling
summary: NIST SP 800-61 is the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication titled Computer Security Incident Handling Guide. It is guidance, not law: it describes how an organisation can build and run an incident response capability, and it is widely used as the reference structure that incident response plans, tabletop exercises and audit questions are mapped against. Its central contribution is a lifecycle view of incident handling, commonly summarised as preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity, with the explicit idea that lessons learned feed back into preparation and detection rather than ending the case. It also discusses coordinating with outside parties, handling evidence, and choosing incident severity classifications so that escalation is consistent. The mistake people make is treating it as a checklist that a team completes once, or as a document that prescribes specific technical tools and thresholds; it deliberately stays technology-neutral, and a plan that copies its headings without assigning named owners, contact paths, evidence handling rules and decision authority for shutting systems down has the shape of a plan and none of the function.

beginner.definition: NIST SP 800-61 is a public guide about how to handle security incidents. NIST is a United States government standards body, and the SP number is just its document label. The guide explains how to prepare for incidents and what to do while one is happening. It is free to read and is used by many companies as a model.
beginner.whyItMatters: During a real incident people are stressed and time is short, so the decisions must already be written down. A guide gives you an agreed order of work instead of an argument in the middle of a crisis. It reminds you to prepare before anything happens, which is the part teams skip. It also asks you to review each case afterwards so the same failure does not repeat. Without a plan, response depends on whoever happens to be on shift.
howItWorks: Preparation means writing the plan, giving people clear roles and testing everything before you need it.
Detection and analysis means noticing an event, deciding whether it is a real incident and judging how serious it is.
Containment means stopping the spread, for example by isolating a machine from the network.
Eradication means removing the cause, such as deleting malicious files or closing the way in.
Recovery means returning systems to normal service carefully, while watching for the problem coming back.
Post incident activity means meeting afterwards and improving the plan, tools and detection rules.
beginner.example: Think of a fire station. Preparation is buying equipment, training the crew and practising drills before any fire. Detection is the alarm. Containment is stopping the fire from spreading to the next building. Recovery is making the building usable again. Afterwards the crew studies what happened and changes their drills. A station with shiny trucks and no drills looks ready but fails on the night it matters.
takeaways: Incident handling is a cycle, and the review after an incident improves the preparation before the next one.
The guide describes what a capability must cover, not which products or settings you must use.
A written plan only works if roles, contacts and the authority to isolate systems are decided in advance.

objectives: Explain what NIST SP 800-61 is and how it is intended to be used by an organisation.
List the phases of the incident handling lifecycle and what each phase achieves.
Describe why preparation and post incident review are as important as the live response itself.
Explain how severity classification and escalation paths make response consistent across a team.
Recognise why copying a framework without assigning owners and authority does not create a working plan.
